# Photodriven Ammonia Synthesis from Manganese Nitrides: Photophysics and Mechanistic Investigations

Grace B. Panetti†, Junho Kim†, Michele S. Myong‡, Matthew J. Bird‡*, Gregory D. Scholes,†* and Paul J. Chirik†*

†Department of Chemistry, Frick Laboratory, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

‡Chemistry Division, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, New York 11973, United States

KEYWORDS proton coupled electron transfer, ammonia, manganese, nitride, ultrafast spectroscopy, mechanism, acridine

ABSTRACT:  Ammonia synthesis from N,N,O,O-supported manganese (V) nitrides and 9,10-dihydroacridine using protoncoupled electron transfer and visible light irradiation in the absence of precious metal photocatalysts is described. While the reactivity of the nitride correlated with increased absorption of blue light, excited-state lifetimes determined by transient absorption were on the order of picoseconds. This eliminated excited state manganese nitrides as responsible for bimolecular N–H bond formation. Spectroscopic measurements on the hydrogen source, dihydroacridine, demonstrated that photooxidation of 9,10-dihydroacridine was necessary for productive ammonia synthesis. Transient absorption and pulse radiolysis data for dihydroacridine provided evidence for the presence of intermediates with weak E–H bonds, including the dihydroacridinium radical cation and both isomers of monohydroacridine radical but notably these intermediates were unreactive towards hydrogen atom transfer and net N–H bond formation. Additional optimization of the reaction conditions using higher photon flux, resulted in higher rates of the ammonia production from the manganese(V) nitrides due to increased activation of the dihydroacridine.

## INTRODUCTION

Metal nitrides are of broad interest due to applications in materials science and coordination chemistry.1 Notably, terminal transition metal nitrides serve as the nitrogen source in both atom transfer and ammonia synthesis chemistry.2 However, the thermodynamic stability of most isolable metal nitrides results in weak N–H bonds in the corresponding imido complexes.3 One approach to overcoming this energetic limitation is the use of separate proton and electron sources that by formation of stoichiometric byproducts incur large chemical overpotentials.3c,4

Alternatively, molecules containing weak element-hydrogen (E–H) bonds are attractive for forming N–H bonds from thermodynamically stable metal nitrides. Those with BDFEs less than 50 kcal mol-1 are of particular interest to promote additional chemistry.5 Various alternative approaches have been explored to activate molecules to reduce BDFEs and enable productive H-atom transfer chemistry. Strategies include coordination to a metal (coordination-induced bond weakening), photon absorption, redox chemistry or H-atom transfer events (Scheme 1b).5b,6 While irradiation with visible light has been posited, photoredox methods have dominated as an effective strategy for generating reactive intermediates with low effective BDFEs.7 These approaches have been used extensively for the formation and cleavage of E–H bonds through protoncoupled electron transfer (PCET) with implications in biochemistry and organic chemistry and activation of metalligand multiple bonds.5

The application of photoinduced PCET to generate weak E– H bonds for subsequent N–H bond formation with metal nitrides has been demonstrated as a distinct route for ammonia synthesis (Scheme 2A).3c Blue light irradiation of salensupported manganese nitrides in the presence of a ruthenium photocatalyst, acid and 9,10-dihydroacridine (H2Acr) as the terminal reductant was effective for ammonia synthesis.6g,8 Related work by Nishibayashi and coworkers demonstrated catalytic ammonia synthesis using a PCP pincer molybdenum complex, an iridium photocatalyst, and H2Acr.9 Peters and coworkers have also applied this approach to catalytic ammonia synthesis using a PNP pincer molybdenum complex, an iridium photocatalyst, and a Hantzsch ester as the stoichiometric H-atom source.10 In all of the reported examples, ammonia formation was observed, albeit in significantly lower yields in the absence of the precious metal photocatalyst. These observations raise questions as to the nature of the photoactive compound in solution responsible for N–H bond formation. Despite extensive photophysical measurements on terminal metal oxides11 and metal alkylidynes,12 related studies on the photophysics of metal nitrides are comparatively rare and principally focused on luminescence.13

The use of acridine derivatives and Hantzsch esters as hydrogen atom donors is also well established. Due to their structural similarity to NADPH, many studies have reported the application of both acridines and Hantzsch esters as sources of either formal hydrogen atoms, hydrides, or dihydrogen.14 Their utility has been demonstrated in both fine chemical synthesis15 and in small molecule activation primarily in the reduction of CO2.14, 16 Despite the extensive knowledge surrounding these reactivity of these molecules, only recently have they been applied to N–H bond formation in the context of ammonia synthesis from the reduction of either N2 or metal nitrides. Despite this promising reactivity, little is known about the mechanism of action particularly in the absence of precious metal photocatalysts. Scheme 2. Here we describe the exploration of the origin and mechanism of light-driven ammonia formation from manganese nitrides in the absence of a precious metal photocatalyst (Scheme 2B). The synthesis and isolation of multiple manganese nitrides is reported and their ground state spectroscopy and electrochemical data are described. The BDFEs of previously proposed intermediates indicate that the formation of either the manganese (IV) imido or acridine radical are responsible for ammonia formation. Using transient absorption pump-probe spectroscopy, the lifetimes of salen-supported manganese nitrides were measured and determined to be significantly shorter than the required lifetime to engage in diffusion-based reaction chemistry. Instead, light absorption of acridine derivatives is responsible for the initiation of N–H bond formation and subsequent ammonia production.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Synthesis and Spectroscopy of Manganese(V) Nitride Derivatives. One hypothesis for the photoproduction of ammonia in the absence of a precious metal photocatalyst relies on excitation of the manganese nitride by visible light to engage in subsequent N–H bond formation. Because only one example of a salen-supported manganese nitride (MnN-1) was examined for ammonia synthesis,6g,8 ligand modifications were explored to systematically evaluate the role of blue light absorption. The related acnacen L-3 was targeted to absorb shorter wavelength light with a lower extinction coefficient,

while both salophen L-2 and bis-phenoxyphenanthrolene L-4 were expected to absorb light of higher wavelength with a higher molar extinction coefficient (Scheme 3). The corresponding manganese nitrides were synthesized either by initial treatment of the proligand with an excess of Mn(OAc)2•4(H2O) followed by a quench with a saturated NaCl solution or treatment of the proligand with 3 equivalents of NEt3 and 3 equivalents of MnCl2(OH2)4 to obtain the putative manganese(III) chloride. In all three cases, these intermediates were used without further purification. The resulting brown solids were treated first with an excess of NH4OH at 0 °C in a methylene chloride/methanol mixture followed by dropwise addition of a solution of 8% w/w NaOCl(aq). Each of the isolated manganese nitrides was characterized by X-ray diffraction and molecular geometries similar to MnN-1 were observed in all cases.17 The geometries of the pentacoordinate complexes are best described as idealized square pyramidal where the nitrogen atom occupies the apical position. The Mn–N distances in all four molecules range between 1.5192(6) and 1.530(4) Å and are statistically indistinguishable. Interrogation of the Mn–N stretching frequency by infrared spectroscopy produced values between 1049–1053 cm-1 and is consistent with a strong metal-nitrogen triple bond for each member of the series (Figures S35–S36). nm with molar extinction coefficients ranging between 160– 370 L•mol-1•cm-1 (Figure 1). However, the signal with the second lowest energy in the spectra varies greatly with the identity of the supporting ligand with λmax ranging between 326–450 nm with molar extinction coefficients

between 9300–19400 L•mol-1•cm-1. These observations are consistent with previous reports by Gray and coworkers on similar salen-supported manganese(V) nitrides. The lowest energy absorption was assigned as principally a d-d transition, while the higher energy transition was attributed to intraligand charge transfer (ILCT) bands.18 These assignments are consistent with the observations described here, where the identity of the ligand has very little impact on the energy or intensity of the lower energy band, but the higher energy absorption is dependent on ligand identity. These results further demonstrate that the identity of the N,N,O,O-ligand does not have a major impact on the manganese–nitrogen interaction.

To verify the impact of ligand identity on redox properties of the complex, electrochemical studies were performed. Each experiment was conducted in THF with [NBu4][PF6] as the electrolyte (Figure 2), as the reductive electrochemical window of PhCF3 is too narrow.19 Analysis of the anodic sweep of the cyclic voltammograms (CV) reveals an irreversible peak between Epa= 0.35 V versus Fc/Fc+ and Epa= 0.41 V versus Fc/Fc+ for all four nitrides. These peaks are consistent with a nitride-centered oxidation, as reported previously.20 In the cathodic sweep MnN-1, MnN-2, and MnN-3 exhibited an irreversible feature at Epc= –2.71, –2.16, and –2.90 V versus Fc/Fc+ respectively assigned as a reduction. MnN-4 instead showed a reversible reduction wave centered at E1/2= –1.88 V versus Fc/Fc+. The breadth of the reduction potential supports a ligand-based redox event. This is consistent with the correlation between reduction potential and increased conjugation (MnN-3 < MnN-1 < MnN-2 < MnN-4). Furthermore, while nearby electric fields,16 electron donating, and electron withdrawing groups18,21 have been reported to perturb the manganese nitride-based oxidation, the ligands used in this study produced only minor perturbations to this redox event. This observation is consistent with other spectroscopic data that support minimal perturbation of the manganese-nitride but major differences in the ligand-based properties. All nitrides following either reduction or oxidation show additional peaks between –1.0 and –0.7 V versus Fc/Fc+ that have been assigned as Mn(II)/Mn(III) redox features from decomposition of the nitride.20 Initial scans with these peaks absent are reported in Figures S38–S41.

Reactivity of Manganese Nitride Derivatives. Having established that the electronic differences between the manganese nitrides are principally ligand centered, reactivity studies with these compounds were explored. Addition of five equivalents of H2Acr to a THF solution of each manganese nitride followed by irradiation with 427 nm light under reduced pressure furnished acridine (Acr), ammonia, and a reduced, paramagnetic manganese byproduct (Scheme 4). Other possible products derived from H2Acr such as dihydrodiacridine ((HAcr)2) or acridinium derivatives (HAcr+) were not observed. These products were precluded from analysis due to the required removal of the paramagnetic manganese byproduct. Reactions were performed under reduced pressure to promote ammonia dissociation and minimize potential reactivity with the reaction components and manganese products.6g When these studies were conducted in THF, MnN-4 produced the highest yield of ammonia at 24% yield relative to the manganese nitride (Figure S6). Using α,α,α-trifluorotoluene (PhCF3) as the solvent significantly increased the yield of ammonia across the series of manganese nitrides. Under these conditions, MnN-2 proved the most efficient with an 85% yield of free ammonia as well as complete consumption of the nitride and generated 2.2 equivalents of acridine. Under the same conditions, MnN-1 and MnN-3 produced 40% of ammonia, accompanied by incomplete consumption of the nitride. In the case of  MnN-4,  a turbid mixture formed rapidly,

likely due to the manganese byproduct being insoluble, which is expected to decrease light absorption. The efficiency of ammonia production generally trended with the production of acridine. MnN-2 produced 2.2 equivalents of acridine while MnN-1, MnN-3 and MnN-4 furnished 1.3, 0.7 and 0.8 equivalents, respectively. Overall, the yield based on hydrogen atoms incorporated from H2Acr to NH3 ranges from 86% with MnN-3 to 46% using MnN-1, which may come from reactivity with either the reduced manganese product or the free ligand (Scheme 4).

Isotopic labeling studies were conducted to confirm the terminal metal nitride as the N-atom source in the formed NH3. The synthesis of the 15N isotopologue, Mn15N-2 was accomplished by using a mixture of 15NH4Cl and NaOH in the place of the NH4OH solution. The 1H NMR spectrum of Mn15N-2 was indistinguishable from the natural abundance isotopologue. Notably a signal was observed at 1054 ppm in the 15N NMR spectrum, diagnostic of a metal nitride (Figure S14). Additionally, the Mn–N stretching frequency of Mn15N-2 exhibited a redshift to 1023 cm-1, verifying the assignment of the Mn–N stretch (Figure S37).  Irradiation of Mn15N-2 under the standard reaction conditions produced 15NH3 exclusively as judged by observation of a doublet rather than a 1:1:1 triplet in the DMSO-d6 1H NMR spectrum (Figure S1).

To support H2Acr as the hydrogen source in ammonia synthesis, 9,10-dihydro-9,10-d2-acridine-9-d (H2Acr-d3) was used in place of natural abundance H2Acr for 42 h and the free ammonia generated from the photodriven reaction was analyzed by trapping as (ND3-xHx)BH3. The isotopic composition of reaction between ammonia and BH3 furnished the ammonia borane adduct (ND1.6H1.4)BH3. Deuterium incorporation was determined using 2H NMR in tandem with the integration from 1H NMR spectroscopy (Figures S2–S3). With the source of proton and nitrogen atom identified, investigations were focused on the steps necessary for bond formation.

Additional reactivity of MnN-2 was explored to investigate understand the mode of activation. Addition of one equivalent of potassium naphthalenide, tri-(4-bromophenyl)ammonium hexachloroanimonate, or Brookhart’s acid as sources of electron, hole, or proton respectively were added to one equivalent of MnN-2 and 5 equivalents of H2Acr in either THF or CF3Ph. To ensure NH3 was not lost upon immediate addition of the reductant, oxidant, or proton, the reactants were added as a mixture of solids and the solvent added by vacuum transfer at approximately -197 °C. The mixture was then warmed to room temperature and stirred for 16 hours. Addition of proton resulted in an ammonia yield of 25% and addition of electron resulted in an ammonia yield of 8%; however, oxidant did not produced no ammonia (Figure S7). As the solubility of MnN- 2 and especially H2Acr is poor in CF3Ph, there is potential for the known oxidatively induced coupling of MnN-2 to outcompete reactivity under conditions of low H2Acr concentration.

One hypothesis for N–H bond formation with the N,N,O,Osupported manganese nitrides involves photoinitiation as a pathway to ammonia synthesis. Either an initial electron or effective hydrogen atom transfer event from H2Acr to the manganese nitride generates a product more thermodynamically poised to participate in PCET (Scheme 5A). Activation of H2Acr either by electron or H-atom transfer produces an intermediate that contain thermodynamically weaker E-H bonds (dihydroacridine BDFEcalc= 69 kcal mol-1; dihydroacridinium

While the first PCET event is endergonic, the subsequent steps are exergonic. Based on these data, three pathways for the initiation of photodriven ammonia formation were proposed (Scheme 5). The first is the photoexcitation of the manganese nitride and PCET or ET occurs with H2Acr from the excited state. A second possibility is that the manganese nitride and H2Acr form a donor-acceptor pair in solution and the resulting association complex is responsible for the initial photo-PCET or photo-ET. A final possibility involves H2Acr as the light absorbing compound and its photoexcited state is responsible for either the initial ET or PCET event. Scheme 5. Photophysical Studies of Manganese Nitrides. To evaluate the pathway involving reactivity from the excited state of the manganese nitride, the excited state lifetimes of each complex was measured using pump-probe transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy. Using a 430 nm pulse to best replicate the conditions of the ammonia synthesis reaction, signals were observed for all four manganese nitride derivatives. However, the signals that were observed did not exceed 100 ps (Figure 3, Figures S58–S73). All of the manganese nitrides studied display bleaching of signals observed in the ground state electronic absorption spectra. In addition, new excited state absorbances (ESAs) were detected at lower energies. The observation of new, red-shifted absorbances without the formation of a new structure is diagnostic of a vibrationally hot ground state, rather than an electronic excited state.22 No evidence for an observable excited state was obtained, consistent with the excited state lifetime being shorter than the limit of the experiment (< 100 fs). These lifetimes were also invariant in the solvents examined (THF, PhCF3, and 1:1 THF:iPrOH) and inconsistent with the observed experimental solvent effect. Relevant to the ammonia synthesis reaction, such short lifetimes are incompatible with pathways involving a bimolecular reaction between a photoexcited manganese nitride and H2Acr in solution.

With elimination of a pathway involving an excited-state manganese nitride, the possibility of the interaction of the manganese nitride with H2Acr in the ground state was explored. Initial experiments focused on the evaluation of the potential of a ground state complex that contains the manganese nitride and H2Acr in the same shell of solvation. Attempts to obtain evidence of a donor-acceptor complex using electronic absorption spectroscopy revealed minimal changes in the spectrum even at concentrations higher than those of the ammonia synthesis reaction (Figures S51–S54). These observations support no major change in the π-systems of the ligands of the manganese nitrides nor d-orbital splitting in the presence of H2Acr. Therefore, there is little impact on the two components in solution together in the ground state.

Photophysics of Acridine Derivatives Relevant to Ammonia Formation.  With H2Acr excitation as the remaining option, efforts were then devoted to understanding the excitedstate properties of H2Acr. While photophysical studies on H2Acr have been reported in the literature previously, these studies focused on the excitation in the ultraviolet region of the electromagnetic spectrum and in relatively dilute solutions.23 It was important to sublime commercial H2Acr to obtain material of appropriate purity for photophysical measurements. Impurities present in the commercial samples had little to no impact on catalytic ammonia synthesis, however for all subsequent spectroscopic studies, sublimed material was used exclusively.

Photophysical studies of the purified H2Acr were initiated using fluorescence spectroscopy. Solutions of H2Acr in THF irradiated at 310 nm produced a signal at 350 nm with a lifetime of 11 ns. Using PhCF3 as the solvent exhibited no detectable fluorescence, consistent with a new potential nonradiative decay pathway (Figure 4A). Predicting the excited

state reduction potential by the sum of the redox event and the excited state energy of H2Acr in THF produced a value of approximately −3.2 V versus Fc/Fc+, which is capable of reducing PhCF3 (Epc = −3.1 V versus Fc/Fc+) to its radical anion.24 As derivatives of H2Acr have been targeted for photoreduction,25 the ability to reduce the PhCF3 solvent is plausible. Acr was an observed byproduct of the reaction with manganese nitrides, resulting from oxidation of H2Acr. In the steps to produce Acr, acridinium (HAcr+) is a potential intermediate. Understanding the interactions between Acr and HAcr+ with H2Acr is important for understanding the mechanism of the N– H bond-forming reaction. Examining the fluorescence of Acr and HAcr+ in PhCF3, Acr was irradiated at 370 nm; however no fluorescence was observed in the presence or absence of H2Acr. HAcr+ was irradiated at 410 nm, which resulted in emission at 482 nm. Lifetime measurements were fit to a triexponential with τ1, τ2, and τ3 being 15.5, 31.1 and 62.1 ns, respectively. Addition of H2Acr to HAcr+ resulted in a dramatic quenching of the fluorescence and a drop in the lifetime by an order of magnitude. The decay was fit to a biexponential of τ1= 1.0 ns and τ2= 4.0 ns. As H2Acr is a reductant and HAcr+ is a potential photooxidant, photo-induced electron transfer is a plausible mechanism of interaction between these molecules.

Spectroelectrochemistry was applied to in an attempt to detect intermediates. Electrochemical potentials of H2Acr were determined in THF using [NBu4][PF6] as the supporting electrolyte (Figure 4C). An irreversible oxidation feature at Epa = 0.52 V versus Fc/Fc+ was observed. By comparison, Acr and HAcr+ displayed a reversible reduction at E1/2 = −2.19 V versus Fc/Fc+ and a quasi-reversible reduction at Epc = −1.01 V versus Fc/Fc+, respectively (Figure S42). Reduction of Acr at −2.5 V versus Fc/Fc+ resulted in a series of peaks spanning the visible region consistent with the acridine radical anion (Figure S44).26 Analyzing the product of reduction of HAcr+ at −1.2 V versus Fc/Fc+ appeared as a disappearance of the signals associated with HAcr+ (Figure S45) and the precipitation of a white solid at longer times, consistent with the formation of dihydrodiacridine ((HAcr)2) derived from 10-hydroacridine radical (HAcr•). Finally, the oxidation of H2Acr was evaluated. Oxidation of a solution of H2Acr in THF resulted in the appearance of a broad peak at 580 nm, signaling formation of a donor-acceptor complex between H2Acr and HAcr+ (Figure S46). This observation is rationalized by the oxidation of H2Acr to the 9,10-dihydroacridinium radical cation (H2Acr+•), which, based upon comparison to known alkylated derivatives, is acidic.6e H2Acr+• is capable of protonation of H2Acr in solution to produce HAcr• that is further oxidized at the electrode surface to HAcr+. This illustrates the low BDFEs of the N–H and C–H bonds of dihydroacridinium cation are comparable to the N–H and C–H bonds in H2Acr. To understand the direct irradiation of H2Acr further, studies then focused on transient absorption spectroscopy in different solvents.

TA of H2Acr was first collected in THF. Samples of H2Acr in THF were pumped at 310 nm and resulted in two excited species with ESAs at λmax = 758 nm and λmax = 513 nm, respectively (Figures S74–S76). The first state was fit to a biexponential growth with time constants of τ1 = 13.6 ps and  τ2 = 1010 ps and a monoexponential decay of τ = 4706 ps. The second state was difficult to fit as the lifetime is longer than the duration of the experiment. Comparing this to an analogous solution of H2Acr in CF3Ph, two similar states were observed (Figures S80–S82). The first has an ESA at λmax = 745 nm that decays into a second state with an ESA at λmax = 508 nm. The signal at 745 nm was fit to first a monoexponential growth τ = 19.1 ps followed by a monoexponential decay fit to τ = 395.4 ps. These observed signals are likely the same states observed in the THF sample. These signals are proposed to be the spin-crossover event of H2Acr from its S1 state to its T1 state. The time constants imply that there is a heavy atom effect or similar impact from CF3Ph solvent, leading to a more rapid spin crossover effect. To see the evolution of the T1 state, longer time scales were evaluated. In THF, the decay of the S1 state is still observed with the growth of the T1 state (Figure 5A). However, when the solvent is CF3Ph, there is no observed S1 state and the decay of the signal at 508 nm was

increased from a mono exponential decay of τ = 13050 ns in THF to a biexponential decal of τ1 = 51 ns and τ2 = 49700 ns with a growth a signal at 620 nm with τ = 6090 ns and a monoexponential decay of τ = 20800 ns (Figure 5B). While these states are not related to any of the proposed species above, the difference in rate of formation of the second excited state is of importance to facilitate the formation of reactive triplet. Upon pumping solutions of Acr in PhCF3 there are two states observed, the first having an ESA at λmax = 557 nm which was fit to a first order decay with a τ = 62 ps (Figures S86–S88).  The second state contains ESA at λmax = 444 nm with additional peaks at λ = 484 nm and λ = 518 nm fit to a decay of τ = 22.4 μs and τ = 23.4 μs for the signals at 441 nm and 514 nm, respectively (Figures S89–S91). While only the peak at 444 nm has been reported previously for the triplet state of Acr,27 the peaks at λ = 484 nm and λ = 518 nm are also likely due to the triplet state of Acr based on the kinetics of the formation of these signals.24,28 The formation of this species is important, as the triplet state of Acr and its derivatives have been proposed to be responsible for the ability of photoexcited Acr to engage in PCET.29 Solutions of HAcr+ in PhCF3 pumped at 400 nm or 430 nm resulted in a ground state bleach (GSB) at 440 nm, which persisted longer than the repetition rate of the instrument. This observation is likely due to the high intensity of the fluorescence of the sample. Subtracting this signal from the data revealed ESAs at λmax = 659 nm, λmax = 509 nm and λmax = 464 nm (Figures S92–S96), which were fit to first order decays of 29.7 ns, 26.8 ns and 34.6 ns, respectively.

As Acr and H2Acr are known to react in the solid state to produce HAcr• and HAcr•′,30 a solution of Acr and H2Acr in PhCF3 was pumped at 370 nm. While at short times the peaks at 441 nm, 484 nm and 514 nm were observed, their lifetimes were shorter than solutions containing simply Acr. Furthermore, additional signals were observed at long times centered at λ = 513 nm and λ = 558 nm. The signal at 441 nm decayed at a rate of τ = 230 ns, and the growth of the new signals was fixed to a growth rate of τ = 200 ns and subsequent decays at τ = 61.3 μs and τ = 73.3 μs for the signals at 513 nm and 558 nm respectively (Scheme 6, Figure S97–S99). The signal at 513 nm was identified as HAcr• and the signal at 558 nm was identified as HAcr•′.26 These species arise from an intermolecular PCET event between triplet Acr and H2Acr, followed by the reverse reaction to ground state Acr and H2Acr. These results agree with previously reported EPR studies in the solid state and show this process occurs in solution.28 Solutions of HAcr+ and H2Acr in PhCF3 resulted in a short and long decay components at 511 nm and 662 nm fit to τ1 = 5 ns, τ2 = 53.8 μs and τ1 = 5 ns, τ2 = 38.3 μs (Scheme 6, Figures S100–S102). These long-lived signals were identified as HAcr• and H2Acr+•, that arise from intermolecular single electron transfer (SET) from excited state HAcr+ and H2Acr. These species then undergo SET to regenerate HAcr+ and H2Acr. Rapid production of insoluble (HAcr)2 at the point of irradiation was observed in both experiments, which is generated from large concentrations of HAcr• present in solution. Furthermore, attempts to study reaction rates between manganese nitride species and reactive radical species using the selective absorption of HAcr+ were unsuccessful due to the low solubility of [HAcr][PF6] in PhCF3 and the high molar extinction coefficients of the MnN compounds. This combination resulted in

no signal being observed after 100 ps. To investigate these reactions between MnN species and unstable radicals, time resolved pulse radiolysis was employed. Scheme 6. Photoreactions of acridine related byproducts with dihydroacridine.

Pulse radiolysis (PR) has the ability to generate strong oxidants, reductants, or high energy triplets from the irradiated solvent. As pulse radiolysis is dependent upon redox capabilities, it is amendable to study the effects of MnN on the radicals generated from H2Acr. As H2Acr has the potential to reduce PhCF3 in its excited state, establishing how the H2Acr+• radical cation evolves in solution is important for determining its impact in the reaction. While PhCF3 is not a common solvent in PR, the expectation is for it to act similarly to methylene chloride as an oxidant due to its ability to be reduced and subsequently release halide anion. To support this hypothesis, a solution of 25 mM biphenyl was dissolved in PhCF3 and irradiated with electrons under an atmosphere of either oxygen or argon. At 10 ns after the pulse a positive signal was observed at 370 nm and 660 nm, where the decay of the signal at 680 nm was fit to a biexponential decay with τ1 and τ2 are 81.8 ns and 3320 ns, respectively. These signals are characteristic of the biphenyl radical cation (Figure S104).31 Additionally, some differences between the oxygen and argon purged samples were observed at λ < 400 nm, which were assigned to biphenyl triplet.25 However, due to the high quantum efficiency of intersystem crossing of biphenyl, it is difficult to determine if this is from excitation of solvent by pulse radiolysis or Cherenkov radiation.

With demonstration that PhCF3 acts as an oxidant with pulse radiolysis, H2Acr was then investigated. Under electron irradiation, 25 mM solutions of H2Acr in PhCF3 produced two states (Figure 6A). The first state contains a broad absorbance centered at 660 nm, which is fit to a biexponential decay with τ1 = 95.6 ns and 1260 ns. The second state exhibits a narrow absorbance centered at 568 nm with a smaller absorbance at 520 nm. The absorbance grew in with a rate of τ = 324 ns and subsequently decayed at τ > 14 μs. The second set of signals survived longer than the experiment window and thus only an estimate of the decay is possible. These results mirror previous results using low temperature radiolysis of H2Acr in sec-butyl chloride.26 The first state was identified as H2Acr+• and the second state as the N-centered radical, 9-hydroacridine radical (HAcr•′). The second state is likely formed by the deprotonation of dihydroacridinium radical cation by remaining H2Acr in solution. The expectation that this second signal arises from


<!-- Page 9 -->


a bimolecular collision with free H2Acr in solution is supported by the formation of the second species occurring more slowly at lower concentrations of H2Acr (1 mM H2Acr PR in PhCF3, Figure S106). This is an interesting result as HAcr• is the thermodynamically more stable species and HAcr•′ has been reported to rearrange to HAcr•;26 however, even at long timepoints the signal associated with HAcr•′ does not decay out to milliseconds time delays. To observe HAcr• in solution hydrogen atom transfer to acridine was attempted.

PR in THF is known to produce a highly reducing electron followed by a very acidic proton, leading to products derived that are formally products of H-atom transfer.31 Irradiating THF solutions of acridine with high energy electrons results in early time points with a highly structured signal at λmax = 650 nm. This signal is consistent with the acridine radial anion, which was previously observed in spectroelectrochemical measurements of acridine (Figures S44, S116). This signal then decays into a pair of signals one broader signal centered at λmax = 515 nm and one narrower signal centered at λmax = 560 nm, which had lifetimes exceeding the length of the experiment. The signal at λmax = 515 nm was assigned as the HAcr• radical and the signal at 560 nm was assigned to HAcr•′. With the production of all of the radical species derived from acridine and dihydroacridine accessible from PR techniques the impact of MnN was evaluated.

All of the compounds that were detected by PR, H2Acr+•, HAcr•′, and HAcr• are expected to have low enough BDFEs to promote donation of an H-atom to the manganese nitrides.6e The response of MnN-2 under pulse radiolysis conditions were evaluated to determine the manganese nitride response. In CF3Ph solvent a signal at 700 nm was observed and did not decay to baseline over the length of the experiment, τ > 45 ms. This signal was assigned as oxidized MnN-2 (MnVIN-2). To see if there is an impact of hydrogen atom source on this speciesintermediate, a 0.22 mM solution of H2Acr was added to the solution and a faster decay of τ = 3 ms was observed (Figure S111). Signals at 660 nm and 570 nm were observed in CF3Ph. At concentrations between 0–0.2 mM of MnN-2 and with time delays of < 14000 ns, both the intensity of the signal at 660 nm decreased and the first rate of decay of the signal are impacted by increasing concentrations of MnN-2. The second decay of this signal was largely unaffected by additions of MnN-2 and may be inhibited by additional metal nitride (Figure S114). At concentrations of MnN-2 greater than 0.33 mM, no rise in the signal at 660 nm was observed (Figure S112). At the time delays overlapping with this change in the first decay (0-1500 ns), there is also no observed impact of the signal at 550 nm due to the concentration of MnN-2. This result indicated that there is a redox equilibrium between H2Acr+• and oxidized MnN-2 rather than protonation or hydrogen atom transfer events. This hypothesis is consistent with the Epa features observed in their electro-

chemistry (Figures 2 and S42). Further investigating the signal at 560 nm showed little to no impact upon additions of MnN-2 at time scales of 0–90 μs (Figure S115). To see reactivity with HAcr• and MnN-2, solutions of Acr in THF were studied with increasing concentrations of MnN-2. Monitoring the signal at 510 nm and 560 nm with increasing concentrations of MnN-2 from 0.16 mM to 0.5 mM showed minimal impact on the growth of these signals (Figures S117– S118). These results indicate that, while predicted BDFEs of HAcr• and HAcr•′ are capable of performing formal hydrogen atom transfer processes, these mechanisms are not viable in solution.

Proposed Mechanism and Improved Photoreactivity of Manganese Nitrides. A mechanism of precious metal-free photodriven ammonia synthesis based on the spectroscopic data is presented in Scheme 7. A small amount of H2Acr is photoexcited to generate a highly reducing excited state. This excited state either reduces the manganese nitride or in the case of PhCF3, solvent molecules. Reducing the latter results in the formation of PhCF2• and F- and H2Acr•+. While this method of reactivity is not observed from direct excitation in TA experiments, the reactivity is likely a minor reaction coordinate and a similar peak at 575 nm was observed in early time points of the PR and observed at late time points in the TA. Once H2Acr•+ is generated, either electron transfer to form MnVIN or proton transfer to form H3Acr+ and HAcr•′ occurs. From the MnVIN intermediate, decay of the signal was observed and is consistent with previously observed HAT events with dihydroanthracene to produce ammonia.21 Alternatively, H3Acr+ was observed in the absence of light to produce ammonia from the manganese nitrides, while HAcr•′ either engages with another transient intermediate or dimerizes to form (HAcr)2. From the 3*H2Acr state, MnN- 2 and MnN-4 are the optimal substrates as they are the most readily reduced and can engage directly with 3*H2Acr. This is also supported by the amounts of acridine produced by these complexes under reaction conditions. This photoexcited species likely undergoes electron transfer followed by rapid proton transfer to form HAcr• and [MnNH]. This is followed by another PCET event to form [MnNH2], which reacts with free H2Acr to produce ammonia and [Mn]. With a more informed mechanism in hand further optimization of the reaction was employed.

Based on the proposed mechanism increasing the photon flux was hypothesized to greatly increase the rate of reaction as this ensures that more H2Acr is being excited that can serve as the source of N–H bonds. To further determine if the radicals HAcr• and HAcr•′ have an impact on the reaction, 10 mol% of Acr was added to the reaction and the reaction was

shorted to 16 h to magnify differences in yield. The reactions of MnN-1 and MnN-3 only showed moderate changes in yields of ammonia with reduced amounts of recovered MnN (Scheme 8). The reaction of MnN-2 and H2Acr at 16 h resulted in a significant reduction in yield to 44% yield with 26% remaining nitride. Notably, MnN-4 showed a large increase in its reactivity to a yield of 87%. The amount of acridine produced at shorter times does not directly correspond to the yield of ammonia. It should be noted that the amounts of H2Acr in reactions that have consumed the MnN in solution have also been reduced. This indicates a competing reaction for H2Acr, the comproportionation of H2Acr and Acr to (HAcr)2.5b Quantum yield measurements for these reactions ranged between 0.029% for MnN-1 and 0.077% for MnN-4 indicating that if chain processes are occurring the chain lengths are shorter than the number of photons absorbed that result in chain initiation.

Furthermore, addition of 10 mol% of acridine to the reaction resulted in reduced yields of ammonia for MnN-1, MnN-3, and MnN-4 with higher consumption of nitride. In contrast, MnN-2 observed higher yields of ammonia at 69%. These results suggest that in the case of MnN-1, MnN-3, and MnN- 4, high concentrations of radical species like HAcr• and HAcr•′ result in unproductive reactivity. While no reactivity was observed between HAcr• and HAcr•′, added Acr could play a redox role in promoting reactivity with MnN- 2 as they display similar values of Epc and in other cases increase the rate of (HAcr)2 formation. ## CONCLUSION

By tuning the ligand supporting a manganese(V) nitride, ammonia synthesis superior to that observed with precious metal photocatalysts has been observed. The mechanistic investigation led by TA spectroscopy established that this ligand effect had little impact on the photophysics of the metal nitride but instead was correlated with the ability of the compound to accept electrons. Accepting electrons either by the ligand or the solvent is pivotal towards the activation of the source of the proton and the electron, H2Acr. Oxidation of H2Acr results in the production of H2Acr+•, HAcr• and HAcr•′, which were all observed by TA experiments, and all contain weak E–H bonds, but are not observed to engage in hydrogen atom transfer reactions. Only H2Acr+• was shown to be capable of reacting with MnN and only through electron transfer. This work is expected to have implications for future work into photodriven ammonia synthesis.
